newsitem.title: UK: LVMH pushes case for 3-way merger plan.
newsitem.headline: LVMH pushes case for 3-way merger plan.

text.p: LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton detailed further savings from its alternative plans for a three-way merger with Guinness and Grand Metropolitan on Thursday, as its chairman came to London to promote his cause to investors.

The French luxury goods to spirits company said in a statement released in London that its plans for such a merger would lead to further cost savings of 65 million pounds ($108.9 million) over and above what the British companies identified in their own two-way merger plan.
Guinness and Grand Met had said that their planned 24 billion pound merger into GMG Brands, the biggest in British corporate history, would result in annual cost savings of 175 million pounds.
"LVMH remains convinced that its proposal creates maximum value for all shareholders," the statement said.

LVMH's chairman Bernard Arnault wants to merge his company's Moet Hennessy cognac and champagne business with the spirits arms of Guinness and Grand Met, setting up a company worth over 60 billion francs ($9.8 billion) in sales.

He wants the merged company, which would include famous brands such as Moet Chandon champagnes, GrandMet's Smirnoff, Gilbey's, J&B and Bailey's along with Guinness's Johnnie Walker, Dewar's, Gordon's and Tanqueray drinks, to be floated in Paris and London.

LVMH is the largest shareholder in both British firms and now holds 11.06 percent of Grand Met after buying more on Tuesday in frenetic turnover while reducing its stake in Guinness to hold 12.3 percent.

Those levels allow Arnault to call extraordinary meetings of both firms and give him extra leverage in Grand Met, which needs a higher percentage of shareholders to vote in favour of the merger than does Guinness.
Guinness and Grand Met have said they will respond to Arnault's 18-page proposal, although no timetable has been set.
Industry sources said it could be later this week or early next week when the two British drinks giants reply.
"We don't expect a positive answer from GMG but we do expect them to leave the door open, perhaps by signalling the sticking points," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.

There appear to be two key obstacles Guinness and Grand Met see in Arnault's plans -- his proposals to demerge their food and brewing operations from the enlarged group and the size of his stake in any merged spirits company, analysts said.

Grand Met chief executive and designated head of GMG Brands John McGrath told the Financial Times newspaper on Thursday that "we have no demerging to do," and "flatly rebutted" Arnault's suggestion that the group would suffer from a "conglomerate discount" if the parts remained together.
He told the newspaper that a combination of the three spirits divisions could enhance shareholder value but only through a merger within the GMG structure rather than a separately listed company.
An article in the Independent newspaper on Thursday quoted McGrath as saying Grand Met would consider alternative proposals to split Moet Hennessy in two.

"Grand Met and Guinness would not say no to the idea of acquiring the champagne business of Moet Hennessy and giving up the cognac side. We would also consider giving Mr Arnault a stake in an unquoted business within GMG Brands incorporating Moet Hennessy and our spirits business," the paper quoted McGrath saying.

At the same time, the British companies have said that LVMH's holdings would leave it with 25 percent of a merged group, while Arnault has signalled recently that he was flexible on LVMH's initial claim it should have 35 percent.
That has led analysts to speculate that there may be a compromise half way, perhaps around 30 percent.
But they added that the three companies were likely to want to resolve their differences and avoid all deals being pulled.
"There are huge incentives to get something going. If these deals don't work out, share prices will fall and everyone stands to lose," said the analyst.

Guinness shares, which stood at 484 pence in May before the merger was announced, were up 12.5 pence to 604 pence by 1300 GMT while Grand Met had gained 10 pence to 627 pence, compared with 441 pence before the announcement of the deal in May.
